title: Sampling Methods and Misleading Representations — Year 9

header.title: Sampling Methods and Misleading Representations
header.subtitle: Who was asked, and where does the axis start?

meta.lesson-focus: Investigate how different sampling methods and choices of representation can support a particular viewpoint or mislead the reader; analyse infographics for visual bias; consider the impact of decreased landline usage on survey data; explore potential cultural bias in reports about First Nations Australians.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: analyse how different sampling methods can affect the results of surveys and how choice of representation can be used to support a particular point of view
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Sampling methods can affect and bias the results of data collection

html.section0_intro: Last lesson you analysed statistical reports and asked who was surveyed and how many. Today we look at how a sample is chosen and how the results are drawn. Warm up the tools first.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's statistics.

Bank B's online advert for its savings account: “Our rate leaves Bank A for dead!” Same two interest rates, two ways to draw them.

Illustrative rates made for this lesson.

In the advert, Bank B's bar looks about two and a half times as tall as Bank A's. The real rates are 4.2% and 4.5% p.a. On $10,000 saved for a year that is a difference of just $30. Nothing in the advert is false: the trick is where the axis starts. Surveys can do the same thing by choosing who gets asked. A phone poll that only rings landlines in the daytime, or an online survey that never reaches remote communities, can support whatever view its designer wanted. Today you learn to spot both kinds of tilt.

Random sample
Tap to flip
Every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen.
A random number generator picks 60 of 900 student IDs
Convenience sample
Tap to flip
People who are easy to reach are asked, so some groups are over-represented.
The first 20 shoppers out of a supermarket
Self-selected sample
Tap to flip
People choose themselves to take part, so those with strong views dominate.
A radio station asks listeners to text in a vote
Under-coverage
Tap to flip
Part of the population has little or no chance of being included in the sample.
A landline-only survey misses mobile-only households
Truncated axis
Tap to flip
A value axis that does not start at zero, which makes small differences look large.
An axis from 4.0% makes 4.2% vs 4.5% look like 1 vs 2.5

✅ Fair picture

⚠️ Could mislead

💡 A choice misleads when it leaves part of the population out, lets people pick themselves, or makes the picture look bigger or smaller than the numbers. A fair choice gives everyone a chance and draws every value to the same scale from zero.
html.section4_heading: Match each choice to its effect
html.worked_example:
Bank B's advert from the hook. Is the claim “Our rate leaves Bank A for dead” a fair reading of the data?

1
Read the true values and the axis start
Look at the axis labels before you look at the bars.
Bank A: 4.2%   Bank B: 4.5%
The vertical axis starts at 4.0%, not 0. The axis is truncated.
2
Compare how tall the bars look with the real ratio
Each bar's drawn height starts at the bottom of the axis, 4.0.
Drawn heights: 4.2 − 4.0 = 0.2 and 4.5 − 4.0 = 0.5
Looks like: 0.50.2 = 2.5 times as tall
Really: 4.54.2 ≈ 1.07 times as large
3
Put the difference in context and judge
Ask what the gap is worth in real terms.
Gap: 4.5% − 4.2% = 0.3 percentage points.
On $10,000 for one year: 0.003 × 10,000 = $30 more interest.
VerdictThe numbers are true but the display misleads: the truncated axis turns a 7% difference into a bar 2.5 times as tall. Bank B is better, by $30 a year on $10,000, not “for dead”.
html.we_do_intro:
A polling company wants to know what adults think of a later school start time. It phones randomly chosen landline numbers between 9 am and 5 pm on weekdays until 1,000 people have answered. Read the chart with the person next to you, then we'll fill in each box as a class.

Many younger adults have no landline, and many people now let calls from unknown numbers ring out.
html.strategy_section:
6bSpot the flawed analysis

A student has analysed a report, but one line of their reasoning is wrong. Read each line and click the line where the mistake first appears.

Report: “Only 40% of First Nations adults in the region use the new health clinic. Based on 800 responses to an online survey, written in English, open for one week.” (Illustrative report.)
1The population is all First Nations adults in the region.
2Only people with internet access who read English could answer, so people in remote communities and people who mainly speak an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander language were largely left out.
3The people left out would probably answer the same way as everyone else, so this does not change the result.
4So about 40% of all First Nations adults in the region use the clinic.

✓ Right: line 3 is where the reasoning breaks.

Why: the people left out are exactly the ones whose experience may be different. Remote residents may rely on the clinic more, or find it harder to reach. Assuming excluded groups “answer the same” hides the bias instead of dealing with it. This is under-coverage, and it can bias a report about First Nations Australians.

Which is the best rewrite of line 3?

  • A: An online survey is always the fairest method, so the result stands.
  • B: The people left out may use the clinic differently, so 40% may not represent all First Nations adults in the region.
  • C: 800 responses is too few to say anything about the region.

★Hinge check: same data, two charts🎯 Pick one

Before the exit ticket: pick the best conclusion. Each wrong option hides a common mistake.

A phone company reports customer satisfaction: Plan X 92%, Plan Y 96%. Chart P draws the bars with the axis starting at 0. Chart Q draws the same bars with the axis starting at 90. What is the best conclusion?
That reads the picture, not the numbers. Chart Q starts at 90, so the bars are drawn 2 and 6 units tall. The real values, 92% and 96%, are nowhere near a ratio of 3.
Correct. 96 − 92 = 4 percentage points. Chart Q truncates the axis at 90, which makes that small gap look huge. Chart P, starting at 0, shows it honestly.
Starting at zero is the honest choice for a bar chart. The bars in Chart P look similar because 92% and 96% really are similar.
Same data, different axis. Both charts show 92% and 96%. Only the starting value of the vertical axis changed.

retrieval.q: A survey about exercise asks 50 people at a gym. Which word best describes this sample? (A) random (B) biased (C) census. Type A, B or C.
retrieval.hint: People at a gym are likely to exercise more than most people.

retrieval.q: In a random sample of 200 students, 30% walk to school. Estimate how many of the school's 1,500 students walk. Type just the number.

fb.60: That's 30% of the sample. Apply 30% to all 1,500 students.

retrieval.hint: Put the values in order first: 3, 4, 5, 8, 10.

fb.6: That's the mean. The median is the middle value once the data is in order.

matchTerms.html: Survey only in English, only online
Remote First Nations communities are missed
Icon doubled in height and width
“Twice as much” looks four times as big

weDo.q: In the population, 30% of adults are aged 18–34. What percentage of the sample is aged 18–34? Type just the number.
weDo.hint: Read the coral bar for 18–34 years.

fb.30: That's the population bar (navy). The sample is the coral bar.

weDo.q: Which age group is most over-represented in the sample? (A) 18–34 (B) 35–59 (C) 60+. Type A, B or C.
weDo.hint: Over-represented means the sample share is much bigger than the population share.

weDo.q: Which change would improve the sample most? (A) ring twice as many landlines (B) ring randomly chosen mobile and landline numbers at different times, including evenings (C) only survey people aged 60+. Type A, B or C.
weDo.hint: More of the same calls keeps the same people missing.

fb.A: A bigger sample from the same list still misses the same people.

checkpoint.q: A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 90. The bars show 92 and 96. How many times as tall does the 96 bar look than the 92 bar? Type just the number.

fb.1.04: That's the true ratio of the values. Measure the drawn heights from where the axis starts, 90.

checkpoint.q: Which sampling method gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen? (A) convenience (B) self-selected (C) simple random. Type A, B or C.
checkpoint.hint: Think of drawing names out of a hat.

practice1.q: A reporter interviews the first 20 people leaving a shopping centre. What type of sample is this? (A) random (B) convenience (C) self-selected. Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: The reporter asked whoever was easiest to reach.

practice1.q: A radio station asks listeners to text in their vote on a new law. What type of sample is this? (A) random (B) convenience (C) self-selected. Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: Who decides whether to take part?

practice1.q: A school numbers its 900 students and uses a random number generator to choose 60. What type of sample is this? (A) random (B) convenience (C) self-selected. Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: Every student has the same chance of being picked.

practice1.q: A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 50. The bars show 55 and 60. How many times as tall does the 60 bar look than the 55 bar? Type just the number.
A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 80 instead of 0. Does this make the differences between bars look (A) bigger (B) smaller (C) the same as they really are? Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: Cutting off the bottom of every bar leaves only the parts that differ.

practice1.q: A survey phones landline numbers only. Which group is most likely to be under-represented? (A) adults aged 18–29 (B) adults aged 70+. Type A or B.
practice1.hint: Which age group is least likely to have a landline at home?

practice1.q: In a pictograph, one coin icon stands for $100 of savings. How many coin icons should show $600? Type just the number.
To show “twice as much”, a designer doubles both the width and the height of an icon. How many times as much area does the bigger icon have? Type just the number.
practice1.hint: Area = width × height. Both are doubled.

fb.2: Both the width AND the height doubled, so the area is 2 × 2 times as big.

practice1.q: Of 400 people who answered a survey, 300 were aged over 60. What percentage of the sample is aged over 60? Type just the number.
Which survey question is leading? (A) “How many hours do you sleep on a school night?” (B) “Don't you agree that school starts far too early?” Type A or B.
practice1.hint: A leading question pushes people towards one answer.

practice2.q: An advert shows Fund X returning 6.0% and Fund Y returning 6.6%, with the axis starting at 5.8%. How many times as tall does Fund Y's bar look than Fund X's? Type just the number.

fb.1.1: That's the true ratio of the returns. Measure the drawn heights from 5.8.

practice2.q: For the same advert, how many times as large is Fund Y's return really? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

fb.4: That's how many times as tall the bar looks. Divide the actual returns.

practice2.q: $5,000 is invested for one year in each fund (6.0% and 6.6% p.a.). How many dollars more does Fund Y earn? Type just the number.
practice2.hint: The difference in rate is 0.6%. Find 0.6% of $5,000.

fb.330: That's Fund Y's total interest. Subtract Fund X's interest.

practice2.q: A phone survey reached 800 adults, of whom 480 were aged 55+. In the population, 35% of adults are aged 55+. By how many percentage points is the 55+ group over-represented? Type just the number.
practice2.hint: Find the sample percentage first (480 ÷ 800 × 100), then subtract 35.

fb.60: That's the sample percentage. Subtract the population percentage, 35.

practice2.q: A council's survey on a new skate park was printed only in the seniors' newsletter. Of 200 replies, 70% opposed the park. Is 70% a fair estimate for the whole town? (A) yes, 200 replies is plenty (B) no, the sample under-represents young people who would use the park (C) no, because 70% is too high to be true. Type A, B or C.

A national survey of home internet access is run only in capital cities. About 15% of First Nations Australians live in remote or very remote areas. What is the most likely effect? (A) remote communities are under-represented, so the results may overstate internet access (B) no effect, because the sample is large (C) the results will understate internet access. Type A, B or C.
practice2.hint: Are remote areas more or less likely to have home internet than capital cities?

practice3.q: A 3-D money-bag icon is enlarged so its height, width and depth all double, to show savings doubling. How many times as big does its volume look? Type just the number.

fb.4: That's the area factor. A 3-D icon grows in three directions.
fb.2: Each of the three dimensions doubled, so multiply 2 three times.

practice3.q: Two bars show 40 and 50. A designer wants the 50 bar to look 3 times as tall as the 40 bar. At what value should the vertical axis start? Type just the number.
practice3.hint: If the axis starts at s, you need 50 − s = 3(40 − s). Solve for s.

practice3.q: A landline poll of 1,000 adults: 100 were aged 18–34 (30% of them support a policy) and 900 were aged 35+ (60% support). In the population, 30% of adults are 18–34 and 70% are 35+. Using the population mix, estimate the percentage of all adults who support the policy. Type just the number.

fb.57: That's the raw sample result, which over-counts the 35+ group. Weight each group by its population share: 30% and 70%.
fb.45: Weight each group's result by its share of the population, not equally.

practice3.q: A bank's online survey found 10% of customers visit a branch or agency weekly. A follow-up survey in remote communities, designed with local Elders and run in person with interpreters, found 45%. Remote customers are 20% of all customers; the online result fits the other 80%. Estimate the percentage of all customers who visit weekly. Type just the number.

fb.27.5: Weight each result by its share of customers (80% and 20%), not equally.
fb.10: That leaves out the remote customers the online survey missed.

exitProbs.q: A survey about public transport phones landlines between 10 am and 2 pm on weekdays. Which group is most likely to be missing? (A) retirees (B) full-time workers and young adults (C) nobody. Type A, B or C.
exitProbs.hint: Who is not home, or has no landline, during the working day?

exitProbs.q: An infographic's axis starts at 70. The bars show 72 and 78. How many times as tall does the 78 bar look than the 72 bar? Type just the number.

fb.1.08: That's the true ratio of the values. Measure the drawn heights from where the axis starts, 70.

exitProbs.q: Explain why a very large online poll can still give a misleading result about a whole population.
exitProbs.hint: Think about who chooses to take part, and who can't take part at all.
